fullName: Polarization Modulation Spectroscopy: polarized hard X-rays for magnetism at extreme pressure, cold and field

status2026.detail: Operational and accepting general users, with on-site and remote access (APS beamline directory, read 2026-10-08). First light came in late 2024 / early 2025 after the 2023–24 installation (APS News, Jun 2026; APS-U updates, Sep and Oct 2024). The first users, a University of Wisconsin team studying flexomagnetism, came in the 2025-1 run (Jan–May 2025), while the beamline was still described as under commissioning in March 2025 (APS News, Jun 2025; APS News, Mar 2025). By August 2025 POLAR was no longer among the feature beamlines awaiting first experiments, and its lead engineer describes 'experiments across three instrument stations' (APS-U update, Aug 2025; APS News, Jun 2026). APS-U itself was formally completed (CD-4), announced in Feb 2026. The source is still the two planar 3.0 cm undulators (APS ID table, Sep 2026): neither the superconducting SCAPE undulators (designed for source-based polarization control over 2.7–27 keV; fully circular light only in the first harmonic) nor the permanent-magnet X-undulator alternative (1 m prototype design, from 2.6 keV) is installed, so circular and vertical-linear polarization still come from the crystal phase retarders, which cover about 2.7–14 keV.

tagline: Twisting X-rays into left- and right-handed corkscrews to reveal hidden magnetism in matter squeezed to millions of atmospheres.
plainSummary: POLAR is a 78-metre X-ray beamline at Argonne's Advanced Photon Source that controls the 'handedness' of light. X-rays from the APS wiggle side to side. POLAR sends them through thin, near-perfect diamond crystals that act as X-ray 'quarter-wave plates', the same trick some 3D-cinema glasses use for visible light. The crystals twist the wiggle into a left- or right-handed corkscrew, or turn it to up-and-down, and can flip the twist about 15 times a second. Magnetic atoms absorb the two corkscrews slightly differently, so comparing them shows which atoms are magnetic, how strongly, and which way their tiny magnets point. Each element answers only at its own X-ray 'colour', so iron, iridium or uranium can be questioned one at a time. The upgraded APS lets POLAR focus this light to 100–400 nanometres, hundreds of times thinner than a hair: small enough for specks crushed between diamond tips to millions of atmospheres, chilled to 1.4 degrees above absolute zero inside a 9-tesla magnet.
expertSummary: POLAR (4-ID; stations 4-ID-B/G/H) is the APS-U feature beamline for polarization-dependent resonant spectroscopy, scattering and imaging at 2.7–27 keV. The source is two in-line planar hybrid permanent-magnet undulators (λu = 3.0 cm, 79 periods each, Keff ≈ 2.6, E1 ≈ 2.55 keV) with a phase shifter, on a windowless HHL front end. In the FOE, horizontally deflecting HHL mirrors (Si/Rh/Pt, 3 mrad, M2 bendable) feed an LN2-cooled CINEL vertical DCM. Its Si(111) crystals are joined by 6H-SiC(0006) (θB ≈ 61° at 2.8 keV). SiC is needed only for polarization generated at the source (future SCAPE/X-undulator): near 2.8 keV Si(111) sits at θB ≈ 45° and would suppress the π component. With today's phase plates, which sit after the mono, the vertical DCM sees pure σ light. An in-vacuum Bragg-transmission phase-retarder tank (C(111)/(220) diamond, thin Si(111)) delivers LCP/RCP (Pc ≈ 0.98) and L-V (Plin −0.80 to −0.95) at about 2.7–14 keV, with piezo helicity modulation near 15 Hz and lock-in detection. For focusing, horizontal toroid/cylinder mirrors at 53.7/54.5 m give 5–35 µm, an 8-stack Be transfocator gives ≥2 × 0.9 µm², and two fixed-figure KB pairs give the smallest spots. KB1 (WD 100 mm) puts 100–200 nm on a 4-ID-G Huber horizontal diffractometer, fitted with a ±2 T HTS magnet or an air-bearing imaging stack for dichroic ptychography and Bragg CDI. KB2 (WD 600 mm) puts 300–400 nm into a 4-ID-H 9-1-1 T vector magnet (1.4 K, 75 mm bore) holding a DAC with interferometry, Raman/ruby and a 7-element SDD, for XMCD/XMLD toward 6 Mbar. Calculated flux is about 1.3×10¹³ ph/s at 10 keV into 114 × 92 nm² (SRI 2021 design value, 20 × 20 µrad² acceptance); the beamline directory quotes the same 1.3×10¹³ ph/s. Source-based polarization switching is future scope: superconducting SCAPE devices (designed for 2.7–27 keV) or a permanent-magnet X-undulator (prototype design, from 2.6 keV).

whatAPSUEnables.plain: The old beamline at sector 4 could focus its polarized X-rays to about 15–20 micrometres. APS-U's electron beam is about 20 times narrower horizontally, so the X-ray source is smaller and its light more parallel. POLAR can now squeeze a bright polarized beam about 100 times smaller, to roughly 0.1–0.4 micrometres. At 10 keV about 200 times more of its light is also 'coherent' (laser-like). Tiny beams allow tinier samples between smaller diamond tips. The design goal is about ten times the old pressure range, roughly 6 million atmospheres, well past the ~3.6 million at Earth's centre; in 2026 the beamline lists 3 million atmospheres as available. Coherent light is meant to let scientists rebuild lens-free magnetic images of domains only tens of nanometres across; the 2026 directory quotes 400 nm for routine dichroic imaging.
whatAPSUEnables.expert: The 42 pm-rad multi-bend achromat (MBA) lattice cuts the horizontal electron beam size from about 275 to 14.5 µm and the divergence from 11 to 2.9 µrad (brightness mode). Fixed-figure KB optics can therefore demagnify to 0.1–0.4 µm even at long working distances (100 and 600 mm) chosen to fit cryostats, magnets and DACs, with about 25–40% transmission. This enables three things. (i) XANES/XMCD/XMLD in DACs with culets and samples small enough for 3–6 Mbar (double-stage or toroidal anvils), with fewer pressure-gradient and gasket artefacts. (ii) Real-space dichroic mapping at 100–400 nm and coherent dichroic imaging (ptychography/tomography, Bragg CDI) at about 10–50 nm, from a coherent fraction about 200× larger at 10 keV. (iii) Weak or diffuse resonant magnetic scattering from small crystals at pressure. On-axis swap-out injection also allows small round ID vacuum chambers. That is the precondition for the planned superconducting SCAPE sources, which would remove phase-plate losses (×5–30) and extend polarization control to 14–27 keV (actinide L edges, 4d K edges; elliptical rather than fully circular light in the higher harmonics), and for the permanent-magnet X-undulator alternative (prototype design, from 2.6 keV). These sources are not yet installed (Sept 2026).
quantitative: Horizontal electron beam size 275 µm → 14.5 µm and divergence 11 → 2.9 µrad, APS vs APS-U brightness mode (POLAR town hall 2021)

techniques.name: X-ray magnetic circular dichroism
techniques.plain: Measure how much a material absorbs left-handed versus right-handed X-rays at an element's absorption edge. The difference is a fingerprint of that element's magnetism, telling us how strongly its atoms are magnetized and in which direction.
techniques.expert: Helicity- (or field-) modulated absorption at K edges of 3d metals, L2,3 edges of 4d metals (2.8–3.4 keV), rare-earth (4f) and 5d elements, and M4,5 edges of actinides (3.3–4 keV). 4d K edges (17–25.5 keV) and actinide L2,3 edges (16.3–22.3 keV) lie above the ~14 keV phase-plate limit and need the future polarizing source (APS-U PDR 2017; X-ray Data Booklet). Hard-x-ray XMCD amplitudes are typically 0.1–6% of the edge jump (Haskel et al. 2007), and the design goal was signals down to ~10 ppm (APS-U PDR 2017). Lock-in detection at the phase-plate modulation frequency (~13–15 Hz) is used, with a ~1–4 kHz chopper for dark-current subtraction (POLAR town hall 2021; Haskel et al. 2007). Where the L2,3 final states carry the moment (e.g. 4d and 5d metals), sum rules (Thole 1992, Carra 1993) separate orbital and spin moments (Thole et al. 1992). At 3d K edges and rare-earth L2,3 edges the signal comes from induced 4p or 5d polarization, so the sum rules are not directly applicable and the data are interpreted more qualitatively (Haskel et al. 2007). The effect was first observed in 1987 at the Fe K edge, a hard-x-ray edge (Schütz et al. 1987).

techniques.name: X-ray (magnetic) linear dichroism
techniques.plain: Compare horizontally and vertically wiggling X-rays. This reveals lopsided electron clouds (orbitals) and antiferromagnets, where neighbouring atomic magnets cancel and show no net magnetism.
techniques.expert: L-H vs L-V absorption via a half-wave (two-plate) phase-retarder setting, with Plin ≈ −0.80 at low E and ≈ −0.95 at high E (APS beamline directory 2026). Probes orbital anisotropy, ferroelectric distortions and AFM order axes. At 4-ID-H, transverse fields up to ±1 T are available for XMLD (POLAR town hall 2021).

techniques.name: Polarized X-ray absorption near-edge / fine structure
techniques.plain: Scan the X-ray energy across an element's edge. The shape of the absorption edge shows the element's charge state (valence) and its neighbours. That shows, for example, when pressure pushes an electron out of an atom's inner f shell into the shared 'sea' of conduction electrons.
techniques.expert: Valence, mixed-valence and Kondo physics in 4f/5f systems (e.g. Yb, Eu, Ce, U) and orbital occupancy in 5d oxides under pressure, measured in transmission through the anvils or in fluorescence. Typically combined with simultaneous XMCD (APS-U PDR 2017; POLAR town hall 2021).

techniques.name: X-ray resonant magnetic scattering / diffraction
techniques.plain: Tune the X-ray energy to an element's resonance and bounce the beam off a crystal. Extra spots appear that come from the pattern of magnetic order rather than the atoms themselves.
techniques.expert: Resonant (and non-resonant) magnetic Bragg diffraction on the 4-ID-G horizontal-scattering Huber diffractometer. The detector arm is split by 25°: one branch carries a 2D PAD at 0.5–2 m, the other an APD with a full in-vacuum polarization analyzer (σ/π' separation). Sample environments include CCR (4–450 K) and He-flow cryostats, a ±2 T HTS magnet, mini-DACs (directory: 20 GPa, 2θ up to 70°, 5–325 K) and strain cells (POLAR town hall 2021; POLAR workshop slides 2023; APS beamline directory 2026).

techniques.name: X-ray resonant magnetic reflectivity
techniques.plain: Reflect polarized X-rays at shallow angles from thin films to map magnetism layer by layer, down to single atomic layers at interfaces.
techniques.expert: Dichroic specular and off-specular reflectivity for heterostructures. A full in-vacuum setup reaches the 4d transition-metal L edges at 2.75–3.4 keV (Ru, Rh, Pd) in fields up to 2 T (POLAR town hall 2021).

techniques.name: Dichroic ptychography and tomography
techniques.plain: Instead of using a lens, shine the coherent beam on overlapping spots and let a computer turn the speckle patterns into a magnetic image. Rotating the sample builds a 3D map of the magnetization.
techniques.expert: Coherent 100–200 nm KB beams (100 mm working distance) on a high-precision stack: ±7° double tilt, XYZ, 360° air-bearing rotation, ±15° tilt, XY and an XYZ nanopositioner with strain gauges. Planned forward-detector distances are 2.7, 4 and 10 m, with Bragg CDI at 2 m (2θ < 45°) and interferometric sample registration (POLAR workshop slides 2023; POLAR town hall 2021). The method follows hard-x-ray dichroic ptychography and vector nanotomography at Gd L3 (Donnelly 2016, 2017). A 3D vector-tomography reconstruction pipeline is implemented at POLAR; it was demonstrated on dichroic STXM data of Nd2Fe14B pillars taken at MAX IV NanoMAX (Nd L2 edge, ~120 nm resolution), not at POLAR (Banerjee et al. 2025). The beamline directory currently quotes 400 nm resolution for 'dichroic imaging' (APS beamline directory 2026).

techniques.name: Spectroscopy in the diamond anvil cell at extreme pressure, low temperature and high field
techniques.plain: A sample smaller than a grain of salt is squeezed between two diamond tips while it sits inside a superconducting magnet near absolute zero. The X-rays shine straight through the diamonds.
techniques.expert: Non-magnetic CuBe DACs with double (compression/decompression) He-gas membranes, using perforated or partially perforated anvils to cut diamond absorption at the 5–9 keV transition-metal K and rare-earth L edges (even 1 mm of diamond transmits ~10% at the Fe K edge, while partially perforated anvils leave only ~0.1–0.2 mm in the beam). Pressure is calibrated by ruby fluorescence (<100 GPa), the diamond-edge Raman shift (>100 GPa), or XRD of Au/Ag/Pt using the Holzapfel EOS (POLAR town hall 2021; Haskel et al. 2007; polartools). For multi-Mbar work, double-stage or toroidal anvils are planned (Strempfer et al. 2022).

scienceCases.title: Magnetism and valence of rare earths and actinides at multi-megabar pressure
scienceCases.plain: Squeezing a metal pushes its atoms together until electrons change their minds: a magnetic atom can become non-magnetic, or a material can turn into a superconductor. POLAR watches each element's electrons and magnetism as this happens.
scienceCases.expert: Pressure tunes the competition between RKKY magnetism and Kondo screening in 4f/5f lattices. Examples: Yb 4f13 (magnetic) vs 4f14 (non-magnetic) valence crossover; mixed-valence superconductivity; Pu and URu2Si2 'hidden order'. These are probed with 4f/5d L-edge XANES/XMCD at 4-ID-H at 1.4–300 K, up to 9 T and toward 6 Mbar. Actinide M4,5 edges (3.3–4 keV) and L2,3 edges (~16.3–22.3 keV) motivate the low-energy (SiC) capability and the future high-energy polarizing source (APS-U PDR 2017; POLAR town hall 2021; Strempfer et al. 2022).

scienceCases.title: Hydrides and the hunt for room-temperature superconductivity
scienceCases.plain: Hydrogen-rich compounds become superconductors near room temperature, but only above a million atmospheres. Tiny, bright, polarized beams can test whether magnetism plays a role in these materials.
scienceCases.expert: Superhydrides (e.g. LaH10, Tc near 250 K at ~1.7–1.9 Mbar) and sulfides need micron-scale samples. POLAR's 0.1–0.4 µm beams and Mbar DAC instrumentation target their electronic and magnetic structure, as well as Fe-hydrides where magnetism and superconductivity interplay (POLAR town hall 2021; Strempfer et al. 2022; APS-U PDR 2017).

scienceCases.title: Quantum materials under pressure: spin liquids, Mott and Kondo physics
scienceCases.plain: Pressure is a clean 'tuning knob' that changes how electrons talk to each other without adding impurities. It can push a material from insulator to metal, or freeze or melt exotic magnetic states.
scienceCases.expert: Pressure tunes bandwidth, hybridization and exchange paths in 4d/5d oxides, such as honeycomb Kitaev candidates and Sr2IrO4-type iridates (Ir L3 XMCD in a DAC was already done at 8 GPa, 11 K at 4-ID-D). It drives insulator–metal transitions in high-bulk-modulus transition-metal oxides and spin melting/freezing in frustrated magnets. Weak diffuse XRMS from short-range order demands the highest brilliance (APS-U PDR 2017; Haskel 2018).

scienceCases.title: Imaging magnetic, chiral and polar (ferroelectric) textures
scienceCases.plain: Magnets and ferroelectrics break up into patterned regions (domains), swirls and 'skyrmions' that could store data. Coherent polarized X-rays can photograph them inside a crystal, not just on its surface.
scienceCases.expert: Dichroic ptychography and tomography at 10–50 nm (reciprocal space) or 100 nm (real space) target ferro/ferrimagnetic domains, skyrmion strings, AFM domains (via XMLD contrast) and polar vortices. Examples cited by the POLAR team: ferroelectric incommensurate spin crystals in SrRuO3/PbTiO3 trilayers (Rusu et al. 2022, coauthored by POLAR staff; measured at the pre-upgrade 4-ID-D, APS 4-ID-D page 2025), and 3D magnetization in Nd2Fe14B pillars (data from MAX IV NanoMAX, reconstructed with the pipeline now implemented at POLAR) (Rusu et al. 2022; Banerjee et al. 2025; POLAR town hall 2021).

scienceCases.title: Strain gradients and flexomagnetism in thin membranes (first POLAR users)
scienceCases.plain: Bending a thin crystal can make it magnetic. The first scientists to use POLAR in 2025, from the University of Wisconsin, studied this 'flexomagnetism' in thin materials for future microelectronics.
scienceCases.expert: APS reports that the first POLAR user group, from the University of Wisconsin in the 2025-1 run, studied flexomagnetism in thin materials (APS News, Jun 2025). A related UW–Madison program (Kawasaki group, arXiv Feb 2026) patterns transverse strain gradients of order 10⁶ m⁻¹ into epitaxial GdAuGe films by helium-ion implantation (rippled GdAuGe and GdPtSb membranes are cited as related work), and lists nanoprobe XMCD among the probes needed to quantify the effect (Samanta et al. 2026). Its own nanodiffraction was done at NSLS-II HXN, not at POLAR. The Gd L3 edge (7.243 keV) is within POLAR's phase-plate range. That the POLAR users were this group is our inference.

scienceCases.title: Interfaces and heterostructures at low photon energy
scienceCases.plain: Where two thin layers meet, new magnetism can appear that neither layer has alone. POLAR measures it element by element.
scienceCases.expert: In-vacuum XMCD/XMLD/XRMR at 2.75–3.4 keV (Ru, Rh, Pd L2,3) and K edges of 3d metals in ±2 T fields on the 4-ID-G diffractometer study proximity-induced moments and spin-orbit-coupled 4d/5d layers. Uniaxial strain cells and voltage-bias cells are also supported (POLAR town hall 2021; POLAR workshop slides 2023).

scienceCases.title: Magnetic X-ray emission spectroscopy at extreme conditions (MagXES, in development)
scienceCases.plain: A new instrument funded in 2024 will analyse the X-rays a sample re-emits, revealing local magnetism even in materials whose magnets point every which way.
scienceCases.expert: A DOE Early Career award (2024, G. Fabbris, $550k/yr for 5 years) funds a MagXES spectrometer at POLAR for magnetism at low T, high pressure and high field, using novel spectrometer instrumentation (APS News, Sep 2024). Its status in 2026 has not been confirmed.

insertionDevices.name: APS30#4 (upstream)
insertionDevices.type: planar hybrid permanent-magnet undulator (out-of-vacuum, variable gap)
insertionDevices.notes: 79 periods (77 effective; 79 × 30 mm = 2.37 m magnetic length, computed). Device minimum gap 9.0 mm, admin minimum 9.17 mm, user minimum 9.4 mm. Keff 2.62 → E1 2.56 keV. 214 kW/mrad², 10.2 kW at 200 mA. Not a 'short' device. A reused (refurbished) pre-upgrade magnetic structure: the IPAC'24 undulator table lists the 3.0-cm period only as 'Existing IDs' (3 full-length plus 5 canted), while the new APS-U periods are 1.35, 1.4, 2.1, 2.5 and 2.8 cm; full-length devices are ~2.4 m (Dejus et al. 2024, Table 1). FDR: 'Linear 30 mm, 2 × 2.3 m at SSC' (APS-U FDR 2019).

insertionDevices.name: APS30#9 (downstream)
insertionDevices.type: planar hybrid permanent-magnet undulator (out-of-vacuum, variable gap)
insertionDevices.notes: 79 periods; device minimum gap 9.0 mm, admin minimum 9.06 mm, user minimum 9.1 mm. Keff 2.64 → E1 2.54 keV. 215 kW/mrad², 10.4 kW at 200 mA.

insertionDevices.name: In-line phase shifter (S04ID:ILPS) with corrector
insertionDevices.notes: Sets the electron path delay so that radiation from both undulators adds in phase. APS-U installed 11 phase shifters with correctors in in-line sectors (Dejus et al. 2024). Exposed in POLAR's Bluesky configuration (POLAR Bluesky config). lengthM is unknown (0 = not published).

insertionDevices.name: SCAPE (Superconducting Arbitrarily Polarizing Emitter), 2 units, NOT INSTALLED
insertionDevices.notes: Planned 'mature scope' replacement for the two planar devices. Pure circular polarization comes only in the first harmonic; higher harmonics give linear (H or V) or elliptical light with Pc tunable to ~75–90% (PDR), which is how 14–27 keV would be covered (APS-U PDR 2017). FDR: 35 mm × 1.3 m (conservative), possibly 30 mm and up to 1.8 m. PDR: 3.0 cm × 1.5 m in a single ~4.5 m cryostat. Fast switching would use ~30 µrad alternating orbit bumps at up to 10 Hz, or ~6 A undulator current bumps (APS-U FDR 2019; APS-U PDR 2017). A 0.5 m prototype (30 mm period, 16.5 periods, 10 mm magnetic gap, NbTi, 540 A operating current) was tested in 2021 (Kasa et al. 2021). The 2021 town hall planned replacement for ~2026 (POLAR town hall 2021). It requires a ~6 mm-ID round vacuum chamber. Installation is not confirmed as of Sept 2026 (APS ID table, Sep 2026).

insertionDevices.name: X-undulator (alternative future polarizing source), PROTOTYPE STAGE
insertionDevices.type: fixed-gap APPLE-X-like pure permanent-magnet undulator with force-compensation arrays
insertionDevices.polarization: all states (circular, elliptical, linear at any angle)
insertionDevices.notes: Four NdFeB Halbach arrays around an 8.5 mm bore (6.0/7.5 mm ID/OD round chamber); max Keff 2.6 → 2.6 keV minimum. K and polarization are set by longitudinal array motion. Switching takes 1 Hz via quarter-period shift, or ~5 Hz with a dual-XU detuning scheme. 1-m prototype design (Qian et al. 2024, IPAC'24). Funded by a 2023 LDRD 'Force-neutral fast polarization switching X-undulator for the POLAR beamline' (Haskel CV 2024). Not installed.

source.canting: None. The two planar undulators are in line (collinear) in the 4-ID straight, separated by a phase shifter (APS-U FDR 2019, ch. 3; APS ID table, Sep 2026). Before the upgrade, sector 4 was canted, with a circularly polarizing electromagnetic undulator (CPU, 12.8 cm period) feeding soft-x-ray 4-ID-C and, in 2002, Undulator A (3.3 cm) feeding hard-x-ray 4-ID-D (Srajer 2002); by 2018 the 4-ID-D source was a 2.4 m, 3.5 cm-period SmCo undulator (APS 4-ID-D page 2018). APS-U gave the whole straight to POLAR's hard-x-ray line (APS News 2020).
source.frontEnd: Standard APS-U High-Heat-Load front end, windowless with differential pumping, rated 21 kW total and 590 kW/mrad² peak (APS-U FDR 2019, ch. 3; APS-U FDR 2019). The design is based on the 28-ID HHLFE. Elements in order: LPPS, storage-ring valve, burn-through fixed mask BTFM1, fixed mask FM2, collimator, GRID XBPM, FM3, photon shutter PS2 with intensity monitor, redundant safety shutters SS1/SS2, wall collimator, front-end valve, exit mask with XBPM2, exit collimator, beamline isolation valve (APS-U FDR 2019, ch. 3). Exit mask aperture is 2 × 2 mm (H × V) at ~25.4 m and the exit collimator is 5 × 5 mm at ~26.1 m (APS-U FDR 2019). Total power when the undulator is tuned to 2.8 keV (linear) is ~16 kW, with ~512 W/mm² on the white-beam slits at 27 m (APS-U FDR 2019).
source.sourceSizeAndDivergence: Electron beam at the ID source point, from the FDR Table 1.1 design (APS-U FDR 2019, Table 1.1). Brightness mode (324 bunches, 42 pm): σx = 14.7 µm, σx' = 2.8 µrad, σy = 3.2 µm, σy' = 1.3 µrad. Timing mode (48 bunches, 32 pm effective): σx = 12.9 µm, σx' = 2.5 µrad, σy = 8.8 µm, σy' = 3.7 µrad. The 2021 town hall quotes σx = 14.5 µm and σx' = 2.9 µrad, vs 275 µm and 11 µrad for the old APS (POLAR town hall 2021). The single-electron photon terms at 10 keV for L ≈ 2.4 m are σr ≈ √(2λL)/4π ≈ 2 µm and σr' ≈ √(λ/2L) ≈ 5 µrad (computed here, approximate). The two undulators sit about ±1.3 m from the straight-section center, so focusing optics see two longitudinally separated sources. PDR ray tracing for ±1 m sources showed slightly asymmetric KB spots, mitigated with defining slits (APS-U PDR 2017).

components.name: Upstream undulator APS30#4
components.distanceNote: Approximate. Center of the upstream device: two ~2.4 m devices plus a phase shifter share the ~5 m straight. Inferred, no published coordinate.
components.plain: A 2.4-metre row of alternating magnets that makes the electrons slalom 79 times, so they shine a bright beam of X-rays. That light leaves wiggling side to side (horizontally polarized) – the raw material POLAR will later twist into corkscrews.
components.expert: Planar hybrid PM, λu = 3.0 cm, N = 79, device minimum gap 9.0 mm (user 9.4 mm), Keff = 2.62, E1 = 2.56 keV at 6 GeV. 214 kW/mrad² and 10.2 kW at 200 mA. Higher odd harmonics reach 27 keV.

components.name: In-line phase shifter + corrector
components.distanceNote: Approximate: between the two undulators near the straight-section center (inferred)
components.plain: A short magnet between the two undulators that sends the electrons on a tiny detour, so they reach the second undulator exactly in step. The light from both undulators then adds up instead of partly cancelling.
components.expert: Gap-adjustable phase shifter (EPICS S04ID:ILPS), set as a function of undulator gap for in-phase radiation. Corrector magnets correct the orbit. APS-U installed 11 such units in in-line sectors. Length not published.

specs.purpose: constructive interference of the two undulators

components.name: Downstream undulator APS30#9
components.distanceNote: Approximate center of the downstream device (inferred)
components.plain: The second, identical undulator, in line with the first; together they roughly double the flux. A future 'polarizing' undulator could one day make corkscrew light directly, but none has been installed yet.
components.expert: Planar hybrid PM, λu = 3.0 cm, N = 79, device minimum gap 9.0 mm (user 9.1 mm), Keff = 2.64, E1 = 2.54 keV. 215 kW/mrad² and 10.4 kW at 200 mA. A future SCAPE or X-undulator pair would replace both devices (not installed as of Sept 2026).

components.name: High-heat-load front end (windowless)
components.distanceNote: Schematic: shown as one unit centred at 20 m. The front end runs from ~13 m to inside the FOE (~26 m), through the ratchet (shield) wall at ~23.6–24.4 m (2021 plan and elevation). Individual element positions are not published; the model follows the 2021 elevation drawing for the last few metres (photon shutter ~22.2 m, tandem safety shutters ~22.7–23.4 m, wall collimator in the ratchet wall) and the FDR element order upstream.
components.plain: The safety gateway between the accelerator and the beamline, inside the concrete shield tunnel. Water-cooled masks and heavy shutters handle up to 21 kilowatts of X-ray power – the heat of a dozen hair dryers – and stop the beam whenever people need to enter the first hutch.
components.expert: APS-U HHLFE (based on the 28-ID design): LPPS, SRV, burn-through fixed mask BTFM1, FM2, collimator, GRID XBPM1, FM3, PS2/IM1, safety shutters SS1/SS2, wall collimator, FEV, exit mask/XBPM2, exit collimator, BIV. Limits 21 kW and 590 kW/mrad². Differentially pumped, no Be window, preserving coherence and low-energy flux.

components.name: Front-end exit mask (with XBPM2)
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.16
components.plain: A water-cooled copper block with a 2-millimetre square hole that lets only the bright central part of the beam through and turns the rest into heat. A beam-position monitor here checks that the beam stays centred.
components.expert: Standard HHL front-end exit mask, 2 × 2 mm (H × V) aperture, with XBPM2 at the last front-end table inside the FOE.

components.name: Front-end exit collimator
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.16
components.plain: A heavy tungsten block with a 5-millimetre hole. It blocks 'bremsstrahlung' – very-high-energy gamma rays made when electrons hit stray gas molecules in the ring – everywhere except a narrow pencil around the beam, which a stop further down then catches.
components.expert: Exit collimator narrowed to a 5 × 5 mm aperture to help beamlines manage bremsstrahlung with small-offset monochromators.

components.name: High-heat-load white-beam slits (4ID-SL-1)
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.16. The 2021 plan shows the slit at ~26.8–27.6 m (scaled).
components.plain: Four tungsten-edged jaws that trim the raw 'white' beam to its bright central cone. At the lowest undulator energies the beam here carries about 512 watts per square millimetre – roughly eight times the power density at the surface of the Sun – so trimming it protects the optics downstream.
components.expert: HHL white-beam slits with tungsten edge inserts. A typical 0.5 × 0.5 mm² opening at 25–27 m accepts ~20 × 20 µrad², used for all flux and spot calculations. 0.92 × 0.92 mm² accepts the full cone at 2.8 keV. Incident power density ~512 W/mm² when tuned to 2.8 keV. Bluesky motors: horizontal, diagonal, pitch, yaw. The FDR gives 432 W through a 0.92 × 0.92 mm² opening with the undulators tuned to 2.8 keV, i.e. the slits throw away ~97% of the ~16 kW total.

specs.maxPowerThroughSlit: 432 W (0.92 × 0.92 mm² at 27 m, undulators tuned to 2.8 keV; FDR Table 4.15)

components.name: White-beam mirrors M1 + M2 (flat + bendable)
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.16 (dual mirror system in one vessel). The 2021 plan shows the tank at ~27.6–29.2 m (scaled).
components.plain: Two super-polished silicon mirrors, struck at a grazing angle of just 0.17°, that bounce the beam sideways and back again. They soak up much of the heat, and their metal-coated stripes reflect only the energies wanted, throwing away unwanted high-energy 'harmonics'.
components.expert: Water-cooled single-crystal Si, 320 mm long (300 mm active), 3 mrad grazing angle each (horizontally deflecting), double bounce with ~4 mm lateral offset. Stripes Pt/Rh/bare Si (5 mm wide each) for harmonic rejection. M1 is flat with a notch to reduce thermal deformation. M2 is meridionally bendable (R = ±50 km) to cancel the M1 and DCM-crystal heat bumps. Slope error <0.1 µrad, roughness <0.2 nm. Absorbed power 254 W (M1) and 118 W (M2) at 2.8 keV.

components.name: Photon mask / pink-beam stop (4ID-PM-1)
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.16
components.plain: A cooled block that catches whatever raw beam the mirrors did not reflect, so only the cleaned-up, mirror-filtered ('pink') beam continues to the crystals.
components.expert: Photon mask / pink-beam stop between the HHL mirrors and the DCM.

components.name: Beam-viewing flags + cameras (4-ID-A)
components.distanceNote: Approximate; shown at the post-mirror flag. The Bluesky configuration defines two 4-ID-A flag cameras, PostMirrBeam (between the mirror tank, ending ~29.2 m, and the DCM vessel, starting ~30.15 m on the 2021 plan, so ~29.7 m) and PostMonoBeam (after the DCM, ~31.3 m). Positions are not published.
components.plain: Fluorescent screens that swing into the beam while cameras watch them glow, so staff can see where the beam is after the mirrors and after the monochromator.
components.expert: Two retractable YAG/fluorescent flags with Vimba cameras: 4idaPostMirrBeam (after the HHL mirrors) and 4idaPostMonoBeam (after the VDCM); used for alignment and for checking stripe and crystal changes (POLAR Bluesky config).

components.name: Double-crystal monochromator (vertical, Si / SiC)
components.distanceNote: Centre of the DCM vessel on the 2021 'Sector 4 2024' plan and elevation (~30.15–31.05 m, scaled; drawn as a drum ~0.9 m across in the elevation). FDR Table 4.16 listed 30.0 m when the DCM was still specified as horizontal-deflecting; as built it is vertical-deflecting.
components.plain: Two perfect crystals act like a prism for X-rays, picking out a single 'colour' (energy) to about one part in 7,000. Turning them scans the energy across an element's absorption edge, where the magnetic signal lives; liquid nitrogen keeps them flat under the heat load.
components.expert: LN2-cooled, side-cooled crystals. Si(111) (d = 3.135 Å) covers 2.75–27 keV. 6H-SiC(0006) (d = 2.522 Å, θB = 61.4° at 2.8 keV) is used at 2.75–3.2 keV: Si(111) is at θB ≈ 45° near 2.8 keV and would suppress π (vertical) polarization in vertical diffraction. The large first crystal has only a Bragg rotation (the beam walks on it). The small second crystal has coarse and piezo pitch/roll for XBPM feedback in B, G and H. Fixed exit with 15.6 mm offset. Stability spec 50 nrad RMS. ΔE/E ≈ 1.4×10⁻⁴. Changed from the FDR's horizontal DCM: the vertical geometry keeps the source's linear-H light σ-polarized at all angles. SiC matters only once polarization is generated at the source; with the phase plates downstream of the mono, Si(111) at 2.8 keV still reflects the σ (linear-H) beam (APS-U PDR 2017; POLAR town hall 2021). The Bluesky mono device has a crystal-select motor (POLAR Bluesky config); whether the SiC pair is installed and in use in 2026 is not published.

components.name: Monochromatic-beam slits (4ID-SL-2)
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.16 gives 31.1 m; the 2021 plan shows a small device at ~31.2 m, just downstream of the as-built DCM tank (used here).
components.plain: Jaws that clean up the edges of the beam right after the monochromator, so stray light does not reach the polarizing optics.
components.expert: In-vacuum JJ-type four-blade slits (Bluesky 'monoslt', 4idVDCM motors m13–m16).

components.name: Collimators and white-beam stop
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.16: secondary collimator 31.3 m, photon mask/WB stop 31.7 m, primary bremsstrahlung collimator 32.0 m. Behind the as-built DCM the 2021 plan shows these small items ~0.25 m further downstream (~31.55, 32.0 and 32.3 m); the model uses the plan values, centred on the WB stop.
components.plain: Shielding blocks that make sure only the monochromatic beam – lifted 15.6 millimetres by the crystals – leaves the first hutch. A tungsten stop catches the leftover beam that went straight through the crystals, and lead collimators block stray high-energy radiation.
components.expert: 4ID-SC-1 (31.3 m), 4ID-PM-2 WB stop (31.7 m), 4ID-BC-1 (32.0 m). The vertical mono offset lets the stop intercept the undeflected white and bremsstrahlung line.

components.name: Diamond phase retarders (quarter-wave plates)
components.distanceNote: Centre of the tank on the 2021 plan (~33.0–33.9 m, scaled; two plate stages drawn as circles). FDR Table 4.16: 33.2 m. This is the existing 4-ID-D tank, reused.
components.plain: The heart of POLAR. A thin, near-perfect diamond, tilted a hair's breadth away from its reflecting angle, acts as an X-ray 'quarter-wave plate' that turns side-to-side wiggling light into a left- or right-handed corkscrew. A piezo actuator rocks the diamond to flip the twist about 15 times a second.
components.expert: Bragg-transmission phase retarders. Plates pr1 and pr2 are diamond with selectable C(111) (d = 2.0595 Å) or C(220) (d = 1.261 Å) reflections; pr3 is Si(111). The diffraction plane is set at 45° to the linear-H polarization so σ and π are equal. Near the Bragg angle the σ and π waves propagate with different phase velocities: δ ≈ (π/2)·Δθq/Δθ. One quarter-wave plate gives LCP/RCP (sign of Δθ). Two plates in tandem give δ = π, i.e. linear-V. Piezo (PI E-665) AC offset modulation drives lock-in XMCD. The 4-ID-D legacy set used 50–500 µm diamonds for 3.2–15 keV and a 10 µm Si(111) plate for 2.8–3.2 keV. Costs: ×5–30 flux loss, 5–30% LCP/RCP intensity asymmetry, and impractical above ~14 keV. Principle: Hirano, Ishikawa & Kikuta (Hirano et al. 1993). The Bragg-transmission diamond plates used at APS sector 4 were developed by Lang & Srajer (Lang & Srajer 1995).

specs.plates: pr1, pr2: C(111)/C(220) diamond; pr3: Si(111)

components.name: Monochromatic station shutter (4ID-SH-1)
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.16; the 2021 plan shows it at ~34.2–35.5 m.
components.plain: A heavy safety shutter, the gate between the optics and the experiments. It lets the beam out of the first hutch only when the hutches downstream have been searched and locked.
components.expert: Station beam shutter (PSS 'SBS') controlling beam into 4-ID-B (PV PA:04ID:B_BEAM_PRESENT).

components.name: Shielded beam transport (4-ID-A → 4-ID-B)
components.distanceNote: Spans ~36.1–50.5 m on the 2021 plan (scaled); midpoint given. Pipe stands at ~37.8, 39.0, 41.2, 43.3, 45.3, 46.5 and 48.8 m.
components.plain: A 14-metre vacuum pipe wrapped in lead carries the beam across the experiment-hall floor, so people can walk safely beside it while the beam is on.
components.expert: Existing shielded transport pipe on stands every few metres (2021 plan), then the small legacy mini-hutch 4-ID-MH (~50.5–52.8 m).

components.name: 4-ID-B entrance slits (bslt)
components.distanceNote: Approximate. The FDR places a mono slit (SL-3) just upstream of the toroids (47.3 m in the FDR layout); the as-built toroids are at 53.7 m. Position inferred.
components.plain: Adjustable jaws at the entrance of 4-ID-B that set how much beam reaches the focusing mirrors – and so how small and how bright the focused spot will be.
components.expert: JJ slits (4idbSoft m10–m13). Order follows FDR Table 4.16; position scaled to the 2021 layout.

components.name: Toroidal focusing mirror M3 (bendable)
components.distanceNote: 2021 town hall slide 'Reflectivities/cut-offs' (toroidal double mirrors at 53.7 and 54.5 m)
components.plain: A curved, metal-coated mirror that gently focuses the whole beam to a spot a few tens of micrometres wide, for experiments that need lots of photons rather than a tiny spot. When the nano-focusing optics are used instead, it slides out of the way.
components.expert: Horizontal-deflecting, 2–4 mrad, 540 mm (520 active), meridional bender 4–100 km. Stripes (SRI 2021): Pd sagittal cylinder plus flats of bare Si and Pt. FDR 2019 had Si (R_s 83.1 mm) and Pt (79 mm) cylinders plus a Pd flat. Focus at 67.2 m (G) or 73.3 m (H). Also suppresses harmonics. Retracted for KB/CRL modes. Slope error 0.2–0.3 µrad.

components.name: Cylinder/flat mirror M4
components.distanceNote: 2021 town hall slide (53.7 and 54.5 m)
components.plain: A second mirror that sends the beam back parallel to its original path, finishing the focusing and filtering out unwanted high-energy X-rays.
components.expert: Horizontal-deflecting, 2–4 mrad, 540 mm, R_m > 100 km, 40 mm thick. Stripes (SRI 2021): Pd flat plus Si and Pt sagittal cylinders (FDR: Si flat, Pd cylinder R_s 69.9 mm, Pt flat). Double bounce with M3, so the beam exits parallel with a few-mm lateral offset (~0.8 m × 2θ, computed). Together with M1/M2 it gives harmonic rejection across 2.7–27 keV.

components.name: Post-toroid beam-viewing flag (4-ID-B)
components.distanceNote: Approximate: just downstream of the M4 vessel (54.5 m); inferred from the device name only.
components.plain: A glowing screen and camera that show the beam just after the focusing mirrors, so the mirrors can be steered.
components.expert: Vimba flag camera 4idbPostToroBeam, used to align the M3/M4 toroid/cylinder pair (POLAR Bluesky config).

components.name: Diamond vacuum window
components.distanceNote: Approximate. A small component on the 2021 plan ~0.8 m after M4 (the FDR window was 0.8 m after M4). The FDR specified 'Be or diamond'; Bluesky confirms a diamond window with x/y stages in 4-ID-B.
components.plain: A thin diamond sheet that seals the ultra-clean vacuum of the optics from the experiment section while letting X-rays pass almost untouched. Diamond barely disturbs the beam's laser-like (coherent) quality.
components.expert: Separates the windowless UHV optics section (front end → toroids) from the end-station vacuum. Diamond (rather than Be) helps preserve coherence. On motorized x/y stages (4idbSoft m1/m2).

components.name: In-line X-ray polarimeter
components.distanceNote: Approximate. Placed on the 4-ID-B optics table (~57.5–60 m on the 2021 plan) following the FDR component order; the FDR position (53.4 m) predates the toroid move.
components.plain: A 'polarization meter'. A thin foil scatters a little of the beam sideways into two detectors set at right angles. Turning it around the beam shows how much of the light still wiggles in a straight line – the check that the diamonds really turned it into a corkscrew.
components.expert: Retractable scattering foil at 45° to the beam, two detectors 90° apart (horizontal and vertical preamps), rotatable about the beam axis for in-line polarization determination. PDR described it as a 90° scatterer, collimator and two photodiodes rotating azimuthally in unison. At 90° scattering it measures the linear Stokes components (P1, P2) directly; the circular degree follows as Pc = √(1 − P1² − P2²) for a fully polarized beam, or by inserting a phase plate as an analyzer.

components.name: Diamond XBPM / TetrAMM (4-ID-B)
components.distanceNote: Approximate (FDR order, scaled to the 2021 plan)
components.plain: A transparent diamond sensor that reports where the beam is, so the computer can nudge a monochromator crystal and keep the beam locked in place.
components.expert: In-vacuum retractable diamond XBPM read by a TetrAMM. It is the feedback source ('Feedback B') for second-crystal pitch/roll PZTs, with a 0.1 µrad stability goal. The public 4-ID status page lists separate position-feedback loops for stations B, G and H (4-ID status page).

components.name: In-vacuum optical chopper
components.distanceNote: Approximate (FDR order, scaled)
components.plain: A spinning slotted wheel that blinks the beam on and off up to 4,000 times a second. Comparing 'on' with 'off' lets the electronics subtract their own background, essential when the magnetic signal can be as small as ten parts in a million.
components.expert: UHV-compatible chopper (design heritage: XTIP SX-STM chopper, Chang et al. 2016), up to 4 kHz, on a translation stage. Used for double-lock-in detection: dark current at the chopper frequency, dichroism at the helicity frequency.

components.name: Attenuators / filters (4-ID-B)
components.distanceNote: Approximate (FDR order, scaled)
components.plain: Thin metal foils that slide into the beam to dim it in steps – for alignment, and to protect detectors and delicate samples from too much light.
components.expert: APS filter box (4idbSoft:filter).

components.name: Bendable KB mirrors 'KB3' (2 T station)
components.distanceNote: Approximate. Inferred from the 2021 plan table position upstream of the electromagnet; FDR: 55.1 m relative to the magnet at 55.8 m.
components.plain: A pair of mirrors whose curvature can be adjusted – one focuses up-down, the other side-to-side – that squeeze the beam onto samples inside the 2-tesla electromagnet.
components.expert: Existing bendable KB (FDR 4ID-MR-3). The PDR noted the bender exists with new 200 mm mirrors and WD ~0.4 m. The legacy 4-ID-D Rh-coated KB was 10 cm (V) / 20 cm (H) and gave ~15 × 15 µm with the toroid. Labeled 'KB3' in the 2023 workshop optics schematic. PDR 2017: 'tunable x-ray spot size down to ~10 µm' (APS-U PDR 2017).

specs.focus: down to ~10 µm (PDR 2017 design value; as-built value not published)

components.name: Incident-intensity monitor I0 (4-ID-B)
components.distanceNote: Approximate (FDR order, scaled)
components.plain: Counts the X-rays heading into the sample, so absorption can be measured as a ratio that ignores small flickers in beam intensity.
components.expert: Ion chamber/photodiode I0 with SR570-type preamp (4idbSoft:A3).

components.name: 2 T electromagnet station (existing)
components.distanceNote: Approximate, measured from the 2021 'Sector 4 2024' plan (scale ±0.3 m). FDR: 55.8 m in its earlier layout.
components.plain: A water-cooled electromagnet inherited from POLAR's predecessor, whose field can be ramped and reversed quickly – for magnetic measurements on films, crystals and lightly squeezed samples without liquid helium in the magnet. Whether it is still offered to users in 2026 is not confirmed.
components.expert: Existing 4-ID-D electromagnet (Kepco BOP supply) with flow cryostat and ruby system. The PDR quotes P < 1 Mbar, T > 10 K and H ≈ 0.8 T across a DAC-sized pole gap, with 2 T maximum at small gaps. It allows fast field ramping and switching for field-dependent XMCD. Sample and magnet x/y/rotation stages. Evidence that it is active: the Bluesky configuration loads the 4-ID-B electromagnet, its KB mirrors and a Kepco magnet driver (POLAR Bluesky config), and POLAR's lead engineer describes 'three instrument stations' (APS News, Jun 2026). It is not listed as an end station in the beamline directory (APS beamline directory 2026), so its user-program status is unconfirmed.

specs.field: up to 2 T (≈0.8 T with DAC gap)

components.name: Transmission photodiode I (4-ID-B)
components.distanceNote: Approximate (2021 plan feature just downstream of the magnet)
components.plain: A photodiode behind the magnet that measures how many X-rays made it through the sample; the dip at an element's absorption edge is the signal.
components.expert: Photodiode with preamp (4idbSoft:A4) for transmission XAS/XMCD.

components.name: Diamond XBPM, filters, slits (4-ID-G entrance)
components.distanceNote: Approximate (start of the 4-ID-G optics table, ~64.1 m on the 2021 plan)
components.plain: The gatekeepers of 4-ID-G: a diamond beam-position sensor, filters and jaws that steady, dim and shape the beam before it is focused.
components.expert: Sydor diamond BPM (4idgSydor T4U) and XBPM for 'Feedback G'. Includes an AVS-type filter box (4idPyFilter) and JJ slits (gslt).

components.name: Transfocator (Be compound refractive lenses)
components.distanceNote: 2 m upstream of the diffractometer (2021 town hall). The 2021 plan shows the CRL at ~65.25 m.
components.plain: A stack of tiny curved beryllium lenses. Like adding reading glasses, sliding more lenses in makes the focus stronger, giving a spot about two micrometres wide – the middle ground between the mirrors' big spot and the nano-focus.
components.expert: 8 stacks of 2D parabolic Be lenses. N = 1, 1, 1, 2, 4, 8, 8, 16 with R = 1000, 500, 200, 200, 200, 200, 100, 100 µm (FDR had 7 stacks). Binary combinations are chosen by the PyCRL controller for energy and focal size, tracking energy (chromatic). Translation along the beam. Spot ≥2 × 0.9 µm², 1.4×10¹³ cps at 10 keV, usable 3–20 keV. The SRI 2021 table gives 2.0 × 0.9 µm² with 1.1×10¹³ ph/s at 10 keV (Strempfer et al. 2022).

components.name: KB1 nano-focusing mirrors (100 mm from focus)
components.distanceNote: Approximate. Computed from the sample at 67.2 m minus the 100 mm working distance and half-lengths of the FDR KB1 mirrors (VFM 275 mm upstream of HFM 115 mm).
components.plain: Two small, precisely curved mirrors – one focusing up-down, one side-to-side – squeeze the beam to about 100 nanometres, a thousand times thinner than a hair, just 10 centimetres in front of the sample.
components.expert: Prefigured elliptical-cylinder Si mirrors at 3 mrad, Pt and Rh stripes (5 mm each). FDR KB1: VFM 275 mm (q = 362.5 mm), HFM 115 mm (q = 157.5 mm), figure error <2 nm PV (<0.5 nm RMS), roughness 0.15 nm. Piezo, picomotor and capacitive-sensor motions. Spot 114 × 92 nm² and 1.3×10¹³ ph/s at 10 keV; with a slit, coherent mode gives 200 × 200 nm² and 1.6×10¹² ph/s.

components.name: Huber diffractometer (horizontal scattering)
components.distanceNote: Sample position: toroid focus point 67.2 m (2021 town hall) matches the 2021 plan (~67.3 m). FDR 2019 had the diffractometer at 61.3 m in a different hutch arrangement.
components.plain: A precision 'robot arm and turntable' that holds the sample and swings detectors around it. It finds the exact angles at which X-rays bounce off the repeating rows of atoms in a crystal – and off the repeating pattern of their tiny magnets.
components.expert: Horizontal-scattering design. The vertical sample circle is omitted, leaving room for sample environments. Circles: τ (whole), μ (θ in the horizontal plane), χ, φ, γ, δ (hklpy 'ApsPolar' geometry), with full 360° azimuth about the cryostat axis. Option 1: open Eulerian cradle, ±29.75° χ-opening, χ ±100°. Option 2: high-precision imaging stack. The split detector arm (25° offset) carries a 2D PAD at 0.5–2 m and an APD with in-vacuum polarization analyzer. Detector rail and filters on the arm.

specs.geometry: 4S+2D horizontal (τ, μ, χ, φ, γ, δ)

components.name: ±2 T HTS split-pair magnet (diffractometer)
components.distanceNote: Mounted on the diffractometer at the sample position
components.plain: A compact superconducting magnet, cooled by a refrigerator rather than liquid helium, that wraps a 2-tesla field – about 40,000 times Earth's – around the sample, pointing along the beam or across it.
components.expert: Custom high-Tc superconducting magnet, Cryomech AL63 GM cooler (orientation-insensitive), 60.4 mm pole gap, warm bore with full vacuum capability. Field actively controlled (no persistent mode); 0→2 T in 5 min (−2→2 T in 7.5 min); homogeneity <0.07% over 10 mm DSV. Axial opening ±6°; radial opening 190° × 45° (100 mm height). Accepts cryostats, mini-DACs and strain cells, with field ∥ beam (spectroscopy) or ⊥ beam (diffraction). The public 4-ID status page labels it '2T Magnet (HTS-110)', i.e. presumably built by HTS-110 Ltd (4-ID status page).

components.name: Imaging stack (dichroic ptychography)
components.distanceNote: Operating position: it replaces the open Eulerian cradle on the diffractometer base at the 67.2 m sample point. The 3D model shows it parked on a cart beside the diffractometer so both configurations can be seen.
components.plain: An ultra-steady, air-bearing sample stage that scans and spins a sample with nanometre precision. It swaps in for the cradle so a computer can build 2D and 3D magnetic images from the scattered light.
components.expert: Stack, bottom to top: double tilt (±7°), XYZ translation, air-bearing rotation (360°), tilt (±15°), XY translation, XYZ nanopositioner with strain gauges. Interferometry registers beam and sample position. Uses for 2D/3D dichroic ptychography, real-space dichroic imaging/tomography (small electromagnet) and dichroic Bragg CDI. The Bluesky configuration also has a Kepco-driven magnet device for 4-ID-G, probably the 'small electromagnet' used for real-space dichroic imaging (inference from the POLAR Bluesky config and the 2023 workshop slides). It replaces the open Eulerian cradle on the Huber base; the two are not mounted at the same time.

components.name: Vortex ME-4 fluorescence detector (SDD)
components.distanceNote: At the sample. Shown looking in from the outboard side just upstream of 90° (snout ~0.17 m from the sample), through the HTS magnet's radial opening and clear of the detector arm; the exact mounting is not published.
components.plain: A detector that measures the characteristic X-ray 'glow' (fluorescence) given off by each element, so one element's signal can be picked out from the rest of the sample.
components.expert: Energy-resolving 4-element SDD for fluorescence-yield XMCD/XAS and resonant-scattering background suppression.

components.name: Polarization analyzer + APD (detector arm)
components.distanceNote: On the point-detector branch of the split detector arm, ~0.9 m from the sample (not published). Shown with the arm at 2θ = 60° toward the outboard side (the plan draws the ~2 m arm sweep there), which puts it 67.65 m along the beam.
components.plain: A second crystal, set to bounce X-rays through a right angle, that passes only one polarization of the scattered light to a fast detector. Magnetic scattering can rotate the light's polarization while ordinary scattering cannot, so this filter proves whether a faint signal really comes from magnetism.
components.expert: Full in-vacuum analyzer with motions 2θ ±11°, η −110/+30°, χ ±5°. The analyzer crystal is chosen per edge to reach 2θ_A ≈ 90° and separate σ' and π'; the Bluesky analyzer list includes PG(001), Cu, Au, Al, Si, Ge, LiF, MgO, Mo, Pd and Pt reflections (POLAR Bluesky config, analyzerlist.dat; a calculation list, not an inventory). Detection by avalanche photodiode (APD).

specs.analyzerCrystals: PG(001), Cu, Au, Al, Si, Ge, LiF, MgO, Mo, Pd, Pt …

components.name: Eiger2 X 1M pixel detector (also Lambda 750k)
components.distanceNote: Variable 0.5–2 m from the sample on the PAD branch of the arm. Shown at 1.5 m with that branch at 2θ = 35° (25° from the analyzer branch), i.e. 68.4 m along the beam. For forward ptychography, detector distances of 2.7, 4 and 10 m are planned; 10 m would reach into 4-ID-H, unconfirmed.
components.plain: A fast X-ray 'camera' with a million pixels that records diffraction spots and the speckle patterns used to rebuild images of magnetic domains.
components.expert: Dectris Eiger2 X 1M (2023 slides) on a rail, plus a Lambda 750k. Used for resonant diffraction, CDI and ptychography. The 'X-ray eye' camera is on the Huber detector arm.

components.name: G/H station shutter (inferred)
components.distanceNote: Inferred. The 2021 town-hall elevation drawing shows an unlabelled shutter-sized box on a stand at ~69.6–69.9 m, just upstream of the 4-ID-G/H wall (scaled). The FDR (Table 4.16) listed a second monochromatic shutter, 4ID-SH-2, at the end of its diffractometer hutch (64.6 m in the 2019 layout). Identity, position and as-built status are not published.
components.plain: Probably a heavy safety shutter at the end of 4-ID-G (inferred from the drawings, not confirmed). Closing it would let scientists enter the last hutch to load a pressure cell or cool the big magnet while 4-ID-G keeps using the beam.
components.expert: Strempfer et al. 2022 state that 4-ID-H can be accessed for preparation, magnet cooling and maintenance while 4-ID-G takes beam, which requires a radiation-safety shutter or beam stop at the G/H boundary; the public status page lists enclosure and shutter states for A, B, G and H (4-ID status page). The FDR had an equivalent 'Shutter, Mono, 4ID-SH-2' at the end of its diffractometer hutch (APS-U FDR 2019). Its PSS name is not in the public Bluesky configuration, which lists only the front-end and 4-ID-A station shutters. Treat as unconfirmed.

components.name: Diamond XBPM (Sydor) at 4-ID-H entrance
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.16. The magnet position (73.3 m) is unchanged between FDR and as-built, so the upstream H positions are kept.
components.plain: A diamond beam-position sensor at the entrance of 4-ID-H that keeps the beam locked on the tiny sample inside the big magnet.
components.expert: Diamond XBPM (4ID-BD-2; 4idhSydor) and XBPM for 'Feedback H' to the mono second-crystal PZTs.

components.name: 4-ID-H slits
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.16 (4ID-SL-6, existing)
components.plain: Jaws that set how much of the focusing mirrors is lit, trading a little flux for a cleaner, rounder spot.
components.expert: JJ slits (hslt). Limiting KB illumination also removes spot asymmetry from the two longitudinally displaced undulator sources (PDR ray tracing).

components.name: 4-ID-H attenuators
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.16
components.plain: Metal foils that slide into the beam to dim it, protecting detectors and fragile samples during alignment.
components.expert: 4ID-FL-1.

components.name: KB2 long-working-distance mirrors (600 mm)
components.distanceNote: Approximate. FDR KB2 at 72.46 m (VFM) and 72.78 m (HFM) for a 400 mm WD; the as-built WD is 600 mm, so the mirrors sit ~0.2 m further upstream (computed).
components.plain: Focusing mirrors that stand well back – 60 centimetres from their focus – because the giant magnet's body is in the way. They still squeeze the beam to a few hundred nanometres.
components.expert: Prefigured elliptical-cylinder Si, 3 mrad, Pt/Rh stripes. FDR KB2 lengths: VFM 405 mm, HFM 215 mm. WD increased to 600 mm for the 9-1-1 T magnet. Design spot 414 × 212 nm² with 2.1×10¹³ ph/s at 10 keV; directory quotes 300–400 nm.

components.name: Incident-intensity monitor I0 (4-ID-H)
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.16 (4ID-BD-4), between the KB2 mirrors (ending ~72.7 m) and the magnet's upstream window.
components.plain: Counts the X-rays going into the magnet, so the absorption of the sample can be measured precisely.
components.expert: I0 detector with preamp (4idhSoft:A1). I1 and I2 channels are available downstream.

components.name: 9-1-1 T superconducting magnet (vector)
components.distanceNote: Toroid focus point 73.3 m (2021 town hall). FDR gives 73.3–73.4 m; the 2021 plan confirms.
components.plain: A huge liquid-helium-cooled superconducting magnet with a 7.5-centimetre shaft down the middle for a diamond pressure cell. It makes a 9-tesla field along the beam and 1 tesla sideways, at temperatures down to 1.4 K – colder than outer space.
components.expert: Split coils: ±9 T longitudinal (∥ beam), ±1 T along x and y. VTI 1.4–300 K, 3-inch (~74–75 mm) bore. Liquid-cryogen cooled (not cryogen-free) to minimize vibration for 300 nm beams. Ramp 0–9 T in 9 min (2023 slides; ~20 min quoted in 2021). Re-entrant room-temperature side bores with Be and optical windows (SDD, Raman). Large downstream window for XRD and transmission. Interferometers track drifts during field ramps. The magnet translates inboard for 'beam-pass' mode to the 4 T magnet. Top loading from a platform and stairs.

components.name: Diamond anvil cell (double gas membrane)
components.distanceNote: At the magnet center
components.plain: Two gem diamonds with tips smaller than a pinhead squeeze a sample to millions of atmospheres. Gas-filled 'balloons' turn the pressure up or down remotely while the cell sits cold inside the magnet.
components.expert: Non-magnetic CuBe DAC, compression and decompression He membranes, on an x/y/z nanopositioner at the probe tip. Beam diagnostics and interferometer retroreflectors are on the holder. Perforated or partial anvils (and double-stage or toroidal anvils planned for >3 Mbar). Directory: 3 Mbar, 8.7 T, 1.4–300 K.

specs.pressureControl: in-situ He gas membranes driven by remote pressure controllers (Bluesky devices ge_apply/ge_release)
specs.mount: x/y/z nanopositioner at the probe tip

components.name: Raman / ruby spectrometer (pressure gauge)
components.distanceNote: Optical access through the magnet's re-entrant side bore on the outboard side (SRI 2021 drawing).
components.plain: A laser and spectrometer that read the pressure from the glow of a tiny ruby chip, or from the Raman 'note' of the diamond tip, through a side window in the magnet.
components.expert: Ventus-series laser and a spectrometer run through Princeton Instruments LightField (device names in the POLAR Bluesky config), with a motorized objective (x, y, z, tilt, rotation). Ruby fluorescence calibrates pressure below 100 GPa and the diamond-edge Raman shift above 100 GPa; the system also serves multimodal Raman studies (POLAR town hall 2021).

specs.calibration: ruby (<100 GPa), diamond Raman edge (>100 GPa)

components.name: Laser interferometers (sample position)
components.distanceNote: Heads on the magnet support, looking into the side bores.
components.plain: Laser 'rulers' that notice if the sample drifts while the magnet's field ramps up or down, so motors can steer it back under the tiny beam.
components.expert: Multi-channel interferometry (FDR 4-ID-EX-8, 3-channel) monitors horizontal and vertical magnet and sample positions perpendicular to the beam, feeding slow correction via the nanopositioner.

components.name: 7-element fluorescence detector (SDD)
components.distanceNote: At the sample, through a Be-windowed re-entrant side bore of the magnet (inboard side in the model; Raman uses the outboard bore). The FDR lists 74.2 m for the detector stand.
components.plain: A seven-element detector at a side window that collects the X-rays re-emitted by the sample, for measurements that cannot be done by looking straight through it.
components.expert: 7-element SDD (Xspress3 ME7 readout); FDR also foresaw backscatter photodiode-array fluorescence detection on the DAC assembly.

components.name: Transmission detector I (4-ID-H)
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.16 (4ID-BD-5)
components.plain: Measures the X-rays that made it through the diamonds and the sample. Their dip at an absorption edge – and its tiny change with the light's handedness – is the main signal.
components.expert: Photodiode/ion chamber (I1/I2 preamps 4idhSoft:A2/A3) behind the magnet's downstream window.

components.name: 4 T cryogen-free magnet (existing)
components.distanceNote: Approximate, from the 2021 plan (~76.3 m); FDR 75.9 m ('small-bore 4 T magnet, existing')
components.plain: A smaller, refrigerator-cooled magnet at the end of the line. The big magnet slides aside on rails to let the beam through to it.
components.expert: Legacy 4-ID-D cryogen-free 4 T small-bore magnet, reached in 'beam-pass' mode with the 9-1-1 magnet translated inboard. Used with toroid-focused beams (tens of µm; the toroid bender sets the focus), since KB2 focuses at 73.3 m, not at the 4 T magnet.

components.name: Beam stop (4ID-BS-1)
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.16; the 2021 plan shows ~77.6 m at the downstream wall of 4-ID-H
components.plain: The end of the line: a dense metal block that safely absorbs whatever beam is left.
components.expert: Monochromatic beam stop at the downstream wall of 4-ID-H.

The ratchet wall forms its inboard side; interior width ~1.6 m at the upstream end to ~2.2 m downstream (scaled).

enclosures.notes: Existing transport (APS-U PDR 2017; POLAR town hall 2021) An earlier draft called it 'U1-40'; that label is not on the published drawings.

enclosures.role: Legacy mini-hutch on the transport line
enclosures.notes: Shown on the 2021 'Sector 4 2024' plan. Current contents and function are not documented in the sources found. Outer height ≈ 2.0 m, scaled from the 2021 elevation drawing (town hall slide 16, same scale as the metre axis assumed; ±0.3 m). ~1.2 m wide on the plan (scaled).

enclosures.role: Experimental enclosure (existing, modified): toroid/cylinder focusing mirrors for G/H, diamond window, polarimeter, XBPM, chopper, KB3 and the 2 T electromagnet XMCD station

Double door on the outboard side. Detector-arm sweep radius ~2 m drawn on the plan. Width ≈4.6 m scaled (approximate) (POLAR town hall 2021). The outboard wall angles inward at the downstream end.
