instruments.name: Phase-retarder polarization control system
instruments.plain: Diamond 'quarter-wave plates' that set the twist of the X-ray light and flip it many times a second. Every POLAR experiment depends on them.
instruments.expert: Three plate stages: pr1 and pr2 diamond (C(111)/C(220) selectable), pr3 Si(111). Bragg-transmission geometry with the scattering plane at 45°. Energy tracking with the mono and undulators. Piezo AC modulation with lock-in. LCP/RCP (Pc ≈ 0.98) and L-V (two plates). Range ~2.7–14 keV. Kept as the polarization source until SCAPE (or an alternative) is commissioned, and planned to stay afterwards as backup.

instruments.name: 2 T electromagnet XMCD station
instruments.plain: A quick-switching electromagnet inherited from the old beamline, for magnetic spectroscopy on films, crystals and powders.
instruments.expert: Existing water-cooled electromagnet (Kepco bipolar supply) with flow cryostat, bendable KB3 focusing and I0/I photodiodes, for transmission and fluorescence XMCD with field reversal. PDR parameter space: P < 1 Mbar, T > 10 K, H ≈ 0.8 T with a DAC. Its place in the 2026 user program is unconfirmed: it is configured in the Bluesky setup but not listed as an end station in the beamline directory (POLAR Bluesky config; APS beamline directory 2026).

instruments.name: Huber diffractometer with 2 T HTS magnet (resonant scattering, reflectivity, spectroscopy)
instruments.plain: A multi-axis 'goniometer' that turns crystals and films to catch magnetic X-ray reflections, with a 2-tesla magnet around the sample.
instruments.expert: Horizontal scattering; open Eulerian cradle (χ ±100°, ±29.75° opening). Split detector arm: Eiger2 X 1M / Lambda 750k at 0.5–2 m, APD with in-vacuum polarization analyzer. Vortex SDD. Environments: CCR 4–450 K, He-flow cryostat, ±2 T HTS magnet (field ∥ or ⊥ beam, in-vacuum option), mini-DAC (directory: 20 GPa, 2θ up to 70°, 5–325 K), strain cells, voltage cells. Low-energy in-vacuum XMCD/XRMR down to 2.75–2.8 keV.

instruments.name: Dichroic coherent-imaging setup (ptychography, tomography, Bragg CDI)
instruments.plain: Swaps the cradle for an ultra-stable spinning stage to make nanoscale 2D and 3D magnetic images.
instruments.expert: Air-bearing rotation plus nanopositioner stack, KB1 at 100 mm WD (100 nm), interferometric registration. Forward ptychography at 2.7, 4 and 10 m detector distances; Bragg CDI at 2 m (2θ < 45°). 3D dichroic ptychography was developed under a 2021 LDRD (Strempfer, Deng, Gürsoy).
sampleEnvironments: room temperature / small electromagnet (others under development)

instruments.name: 9-1-1 T magnet + DAC extreme-conditions spectroscopy instrument
instruments.plain: The 'extreme corner' of POLAR: crushing pressure, near-absolute-zero cold and an intense magnetic field, all at once.
instruments.expert: Cryogenic Ltd 9-1-1 T vector magnet, 1.4–300 K VTI, 75 mm bore. The CuBe DAC with double membrane sits on an x/y/z nanopositioner. Interferometers. Raman/ruby via side bore. 7-element SDD via a Be side window. Downstream window for XRD. Magnet on a heavy-load motorized table (x, y, rotation, height). KB2 at 600 mm WD. XMCD at up to 9 T; XMLD at 1 T transverse.
sampleEnvironments: DAC with He membranes (3 Mbar operational, 6 Mbar goal)

instruments.name: 4 T cryogen-free magnet
instruments.plain: An older, refrigerator-cooled magnet at the end of the line.
instruments.expert: Existing small-bore 4 T magnet, used in beam-pass mode.

instruments.name: MagXES spectrometer (planned)
instruments.plain: A future instrument that reads magnetism from the X-rays a sample emits.
instruments.expert: Magnetic X-ray emission spectroscopy at low T, high pressure and high field. Funded by a 2024 DOE Early Career award to G. Fabbris. Design, location and schedule are not published.

geometryNotes: One straight, non-canted line from the 4-ID straight, with two collinear planar undulators separated by a phase shifter. Before the upgrade, sector 4 was canted, feeding soft-x-ray 4-ID-C (CPU undulator) and 4-ID-E/XTIP plus hard-x-ray 4-ID-D. Those branches are gone, and POLAR uses the whole straight (APS News 2020; POLAR town hall 2021; Srajer 2002). Beam offsets along the line, all small for a 3D model: (1) The HHL mirror pair deflects horizontally (3 mrad grazing angle each) and returns the beam parallel with ~4 mm lateral offset; the direction (inboard/outboard) is not published. (2) The vertical DCM has a fixed 15.6 mm vertical offset, assumed upward. (3) The phase plates transmit the beam straight through, with each plate's diffraction plane tilted 45° about the beam. (4) The M3/M4 toroid/cylinder pair (53.7/54.5 m) deflects horizontally (2–4 mrad grazing angle each) and returns the beam parallel with a few-mm offset. The pair retracts for KB/CRL modes, so the downstream beam axis differs slightly between toroid and KB modes. (5) Each KB pair has the VFM upstream of the HFM, at 3 mrad each. Enclosures (scaled from the 2021 'Sector 4 2024' plan, ±0.3 m): 4-ID-A 24.4–36.1 m (inside the hall, against the ratchet wall); shielded transport 36.1–50.5 m; mini-hutch 4-ID-MH 50.5–52.8 m; 4-ID-B 52.8–63.3 m (~2.5 m wide, existing, tapered at its downstream end); 4-ID-G 63.5–70.0 m and 4-ID-H 70.0–77.7 m (both new, ~4.6 m wide, H's outboard wall angled inward at the downstream end). All are on the experiment-hall floor (no long-beamline building). The control room sits on the outboard side alongside B (2021 plan: racks level with B's upstream wall, desks at ~60–63 m), next to the existing XTIP rooms. Outboard double doors on B, G and H; an extra double door at H's downstream inboard corner; a staircase and loading platform beside the 9-1-1 magnet; the 9-1-1 magnet translates inboard for beam-pass. The neighbouring 5-BM hutches lie on the inboard side. Note the hutch-name churn: in the PDR (2017) the instruments were in 4-ID-B and 4-ID-D; in the FDR (2019) the SOE was 4-ID-E and the instruments were in 4-ID-B (diffractometer at 61.3 m) and 4-ID-G (magnet at 73.3 m); as built (2021 design onward) the diffractometer is in new 4-ID-G at ~67.2 m and the magnet in new 4-ID-H at 73.3 m (APS-U FDR 2019; APS-U PDR 2017; POLAR town hall 2021). Schematic hints for the unpublished offset directions: the 2021 town-hall layout cartoon (slide 16) draws the DCM with the beam stepping up between the crystals (upward offset) and the M1/M2 pair stepping the beam toward the ring (inboard). It is a cartoon, not an engineering drawing. Hutch heights scaled from the 2021 elevation (slide 16): 4-ID-A and 4-ID-B ≈ 3.4 m, 4-ID-MH ≈ 2.0 m, 4-ID-G ≈ 4.2 m, 4-ID-H ≈ 6.2 m; beam height ≈ 1.4 m above the floor (all ±0.3 m). 3D model: one straight line. The 4 mm (HHL mirrors), 15.6 mm (DCM) and few-mm (toroid) offsets are too small to see at hall scale and are not drawn, but the mirrors are mounted the way the cartoon implies (M1 outboard of the beam, deflecting inboard). Positions follow the 2021 plan where it differs from the FDR table (DCM 30.6 m, phase retarders 33.45 m). Drawing liberties, for legibility: hutches are cut-away glass rooms whose near wall and roof are left out; the phase-retarder plates are drawn about 7× real size in an open-topped tank, with the 45° roll of their diffraction plane drawn at 225° (optically the same); the 9-1-1 T cryostat is see-through and its 9 T split pair has a wedge cut away to show the DAC; the DAC anvils are drawn ~2× size; the imaging stack is parked on a cart beside the diffractometer; the detector arm is shown at 2θ = 60°/35°; the polarization arrows along the beam have a 0.32 m period and slowed helicity flips.

interactiveIdeas.title: Make it twist: the diamond quarter-wave plate
interactiveIdeas.concept: Visitors turn a dial that tilts a virtual diamond plate a few tens of arcseconds off its Bragg angle. Two arrows (σ and π components, set at 45°) slip out of step, and the output field traces a line, then an ellipse, then a circle; crossing zero offset reverses the handedness. A 'flip' button wiggles the piezo at 15 Hz and the corkscrew alternates. An energy slider shows the needed offset shrinking at higher energy, until above ~14 keV the plate stops working well.
interactiveIdeas.whatUserLearns: How a perfect crystal changes linear into circular polarization, why helicity can be flipped mechanically, and why POLAR wants a polarizing undulator for 14–27 keV.
interactiveIdeas.physicsToGetRight: Bragg-transmission phase retarder: δ(Δθ) = (π/2)·Δθq/Δθ, with quarter-wave offset Δθq = 2·t·cosθB·r_e²·λ³·Re(F_h·F_h̄)/(π²·V²) (form used in APS-4ID-POLAR's Pharet calculator). Example computed here: C(111), t = 500 µm, 10 keV (θB = 17.5°, |F|² = 32 f², f_C ≈ 3.0, V = 45.4 Å³) gives Δθq ≈ 2×10⁻⁴ rad ≈ 42″. Pc = sin δ; ±Δθ gives opposite helicity. Two plates (δ = π) give linear-V. The degree of circular polarization degrades when angular divergence and the mono bandwidth (ΔE/E ≈ 1.4×10⁻⁴ maps to Δθ = tanθB·ΔE/E) are not ≪ Δθ. Transmission falls by ×5–30 over 2.8–14 keV, and LCP/RCP intensities differ by 5–30% (Haskel 2018; APS-U PDR 2017). The plate's scattering plane must be at 45° to the incident polarization.

interactiveIdeas.title: The magnetic handshake: XMCD at an absorption edge
interactiveIdeas.concept: Visitors pick an element (Fe K, Gd L3, Ir L3, U M5) and a magnetized sample. Two absorption curves for left and right helicity appear; their difference reveals the magnet. Flipping the magnetic field (or helicity) inverts the difference. A noise slider shows why 15 Hz switching with lock-in detection beats slow scans.
interactiveIdeas.whatUserLearns: Element-specific magnetism, why the energy must be tuned to an edge, and how scientists dig sub-percent signals out of noise.
interactiveIdeas.physicsToGetRight: μ± = μ0·(1 ± Pc·cosφ·A(E)), where φ is the angle between helicity and magnetization. Hard-x-ray XMCD amplitudes are 0.1–6% of the edge jump (Haskel et al. 2007); POLAR's design goal was down to ~10 ppm (APS-U PDR 2017). Sum rules at L2,3: m_orb ∝ ∫(ΔμL3 + ΔμL2), m_spin + 7⟨T_z⟩ ∝ ∫ΔμL3 − 2∫ΔμL2 (Thole et al. 1992). Artefact check: a 0.1 µrad beam-angle change at 8 keV shifts Si(111) energy by ~3 meV (APS-U PDR 2017), so the polarization should be switched at every energy point. Real edge energies: Fe K 7.112, Gd L3 7.243, Ir L3 11.215, U M5 3.552 keV (X-ray Data Booklet).

interactiveIdeas.title: Squeeze it: beam size vs pressure in a diamond anvil cell
interactiveIdeas.concept: A two-diamond press with a culet-size slider. As the visitor shrinks the tips, the pressure gauge climbs (100 GPa = 1 Mbar ≈ 0.6 eV/Å³, since 1 eV/Å³ ≈ 160 GPa; ~3.6 Mbar at Earth's centre), but the sample shrinks too. Overlaid beams compare the old ~15 µm spot, which spills onto the metal gasket, with POLAR's 0.3 µm spot, which fits. Toggling perforated anvils shows how much more X-ray light gets through.
interactiveIdeas.whatUserLearns: Why 'smaller beam = higher pressure', how POLAR extends the pressure range about tenfold, and why hard X-rays are needed to see through diamond.
interactiveIdeas.physicsToGetRight: P = F/A, so the reachable P rises steeply as culet diameter falls. Perforated anvils need ~2× smaller culets for the same pressure (APS-U PDR 2017). 3–4 Mbar requires ~1 µm beams (APS-U PDR 2017); the PDR (2017) treats 6–7 Mbar as the practical limit of static compression (APS-U PDR 2017); double-stage cells have claimed higher (~1 TPa, Dubrovinskaia et al. 2016, cited in POLAR town hall 2021), but on tiny samples and with debated pressure calibration. Transmission T = exp(−μL): a 100 µm diamond attenuates soft X-rays enormously (Haskel et al. 2007 quote >10¹² for 0.5–1.5 keV; NIST data give ~5×10¹⁰ at 1.5 keV and ~10³⁴ at 1 keV), while a 1 mm diamond attenuates Fe K-edge (7.1 keV) X-rays only ~10× (Haskel et al. 2007; NIST attenuation tables). Partially perforated anvils leave ~0.1–0.2 mm of diamond (Haskel et al. 2007). Pressure is read with ruby (<100 GPa) or the diamond Raman edge (>100 GPa) (POLAR town hall 2021).

interactiveIdeas.title: Edge finder: which elements can POLAR 'talk' to?
interactiveIdeas.concept: An interactive periodic table. Clicking an element shows its K, L or M edges inside 2.7–27 keV and which polarization tool works there: phase plates at 2.7–14 keV; no circular polarization above ~14 keV until a polarizing undulator such as SCAPE arrives (and then elliptical, Pc ~75–90%, in the higher harmonics); the SiC crystals near 2.8 keV. It highlights the rare-earth L3 edges (5.5–9.2 keV; L2 up to 10.3 keV), 5d L3 edges (9.6–11.9 keV; L2 up to 13.7 keV), actinide M4,5 edges (3.3–4 keV) and actinide L2,3 edges (16.3–22.3 keV).
interactiveIdeas.whatUserLearns: Resonant X-ray techniques are element-specific; the energy window determines which science is possible.
interactiveIdeas.physicsToGetRight: Use tabulated edges (X-ray Data Booklet), e.g. Ru L3 2.838, Pd L3 3.173, U M4 3.728, Ce L3 5.723, Gd L3 7.243, Yb L3 8.944, Ir L3 11.215, Pt L3 11.564, U L3 17.166, Pu L3 18.057, Ru K 22.117 keV. Undulator: E1 [keV] = 0.950·E²[GeV]/(λu[cm]·(1 + K²/2)) gives ≈ 2.57 keV at K = 2.62 (the ID table lists 2.56 keV), λu = 3 cm, 6 GeV. Higher energies come from odd harmonics.

interactiveIdeas.title: The 45-degree trap: why POLAR needs silicon carbide crystals
interactiveIdeas.concept: Visitors rotate a monochromator crystal. A polarization-factor meter shows the π (in-plane) component reflected falling to zero as the Bragg angle passes 45° (Si(111) at ~2.8 keV). Swapping to 6H-SiC(0006) moves the angle to 61.4° and the light survives.
interactiveIdeas.whatUserLearns: Crystals act as polarizers near 45°, a key design constraint for measuring 4d metals (Ru, Rh, Pd) with polarized light.
interactiveIdeas.physicsToGetRight: Kinematic polarization factor: σ → 1, π → |cos2θB|. Dynamical π Darwin width scales with |cos2θB|. Si(111) d = 3.1356 Å gives θB = 45° at 2.796 keV. 6H-SiC(0006) d = 2.522 Å gives θB = 61.4° at 2.8 keV. SiC(0006) Darwin width ~0.29 eV, peak reflectivity ~74% at 2.8 keV (APS-U PDR 2017; Strempfer et al. 2022; POLAR town hall 2021). This matters for source-generated L-V or circular light. For phase-plate polarization, which is generated after the mono, it matters only through the vertical DCM keeping the source's linear-H as σ.

interactiveIdeas.title: Lens-less magnetic camera: dichroic ptychography
interactiveIdeas.concept: Visitors scan a coherent spot across a hidden pattern of magnetic domains. Each position gives a speckle pattern; pressing 'reconstruct' runs a toy iterative algorithm. Images taken with left and right helicity are subtracted to reveal the domains. A coherence slider (old APS vs APS-U) shows the reconstruction failing without coherence.
interactiveIdeas.whatUserLearns: Why coherence (laser-like light) from APS-U enables imaging finer than the beam itself, and how circular dichroism adds magnetic contrast.
interactiveIdeas.physicsToGetRight: Overlap ≥60% between scan positions. Resolution ≈ λ·z/(N·p), limited by detector NA and dose, not beam size. Coherent fraction per plane ≈ (λ/4π)/(Σ·Σ'). APS-U gives ~200× gain at 10 keV (POLAR workshop slides 2023). POLAR coherent flux is 1.6×10¹² ph/s in 200 nm (Strempfer et al. 2022). The magnetic contrast is the difference of complex transmission for ±helicity; for 3D vector tomography, at least two rotation axes are needed (Donnelly et al. 2017).

interactiveIdeas.title: Polarization switching race
interactiveIdeas.concept: A timeline game comparing ways to flip X-ray helicity: the 2002-era soft-x-ray CPU (~5 minutes), diamond phase plates on a piezo (~13–40 Hz), SCAPE orbit bumps (≥10 Hz planned) and the X-undulator (1–5 Hz). Visitors see how slow switching lets drifts masquerade as magnetic signals.
interactiveIdeas.whatUserLearns: Measurement design: modulate the thing you want to measure faster than everything that drifts.
interactiveIdeas.physicsToGetRight: CPU ~5 min helicity switch in 2002 (Srajer 2002). Phase plates 12.7–15 Hz typical (Haskel et al. 2007; POLAR town hall 2021), up to 40 Hz reported (Srajer 2002). SCAPE orbit-bump scheme: ~30 µrad bumps, ≥95% polarization purity, 10 Hz design (APS-U PDR 2017; POLAR town hall 2021). X-undulator: 7.5 mm quarter-period motion at 1 Hz, or 5 Hz with dual-XU detuning (Qian et al. 2024).

funFacts: POLAR flips the 'handedness' of its X-rays by rocking a thin diamond with a piezo actuator: about 15 times per second today (POLAR town hall 2021), and 12.7 Hz in the 2007 high-pressure instrument (Haskel et al. 2007).
In 2002, switching the helicity of sector 4's soft-x-ray circularly polarizing undulator took about 5 minutes (Srajer 2002).
The 9-1-1 T magnet is deliberately cooled with liquid helium instead of a cryogen-free cryocooler, because a cryocooler's vibrations would blur a 300 nm beam (Strempfer et al. 2022).

Diamond is nearly transparent to POLAR's hard X-rays: 1 mm of diamond dims the beam only ~10× at the iron edge (7.1 keV), while just 0.1 mm stops soft X-rays almost completely (by ~5×10¹⁰ at 1.5 keV and ~10³⁴ at 1 keV) (Haskel et al. 2007; NIST attenuation tables).
Before the upgrade, POLAR's predecessor 4-ID-D was described as the only hard-x-ray XMCD beamline in the US and was oversubscribed 3–4× (APS-U PDR 2017).
POLAR's goal pressure, ~6 Mbar, is about 1.6 times the pressure at the centre of the Earth (~3.6 Mbar) (POLAR town hall 2021; PREM, Dziewonski & Anderson 1981).

A wobble of just 0.1 microradian in the X-ray source shifts the monochromator energy by ~3 meV at 8 keV, enough to fake a magnetic signal if the polarization is not switched at every energy point (APS-U PDR 2017).

The two undulators together would radiate about 20.6 kW at their 9.0 mm design minimum gap, close to the 21 kW limit of the high-heat-load front end; users are limited to gaps of ≥9.1–9.4 mm (APS ID table, Sep 2026; APS-U FDR 2019, ch. 3).

POLAR's hutches were renamed twice during design. The experiments moved from '4-ID-B/4-ID-D' (2017) to '4-ID-B/4-ID-G' (2019) to the built '4-ID-G/4-ID-H' (APS-U PDR 2017; APS-U FDR 2019; POLAR town hall 2021).
POLAR was selected for the APS-U scope in July 2016, after a proposal by a team of 15 scientists from US universities and national labs (POLAR town hall 2021; Haskel CV 2024).
The first scientists to use POLAR, in the January–May 2025 run, came from the University of Wisconsin to study flexomagnetism, which is magnetism created by bending (APS News, Jun 2025).
Planned ptychography detector distances reach 10 m, longer than the 4-ID-G hutch itself (POLAR workshop slides 2023).
XMCD was first observed in 1987 at the iron K edge, a hard-x-ray absorption edge of the same kind POLAR uses every day (Schütz et al. 1987).
POLAR's First Experiments Workshop on 28 June 2023 was the first in the APS-U series of feature-beamline 'first experiments' workshops (APS News, Apr 2023).

openQuestions: As-built component positions in 4-ID-B/G/H are not published in a table. The diffractometer (67.2 m) and magnet (73.3 m) positions come from the 2021 town-hall slides and plan. Positions of the B-table components (window, polarimeter, XBPM, chopper, KB3) and of KB1 and KB2 are inferred from the FDR order and scaled from the plan drawing (±0.5 m).

The FDR (2019) put the diffractometer at 61.3 m in an enlarged 4-ID-B and the toroids at 48 and 50 m in a new 4-ID-E. The 2021 redesign moved the toroids to 53.7/54.5 m and the instruments into new 4-ID-G/H. We could not confirm that the as-built layout matches the 2021 plan in every detail.

Source upgrade: the FDR planned two in-line SCAPE devices after the project, and the town hall timeline put the replacement around 2026. The Sep 2026 ID table still shows planar APS30#4/#9. A 2023 LDRD funded a permanent-magnet 'X-undulator' for POLAR. Which device (if any) will be installed, and when, is unknown. Both need a small round vacuum chamber instead of the standard 6.3 × 16 mm elliptical APS-U IDVC.
Whether the APS30 devices are refurbished pre-upgrade structures or new is inferred, not stated.
Directions of the lateral beam offsets: HHLM ~4 mm and toroid pair a few mm horizontally (inboard or outboard?); DCM 15.6 mm vertical offset (assumed upward).
Phase-plate details at POLAR (diamond thicknesses, which plates are in pr1/pr2, actual modulation frequency in user mode) are not published. The 15 Hz figure comes from 2021 planning slides.
The status of the 4-ID-B 2 T electromagnet station in user operation is unclear: it is configured in Bluesky but not listed as an endstation in the beamline directory.
Achieved pressure (directory: 3 Mbar) vs the 6 Mbar design goal; magnet field with DAC (directory 8.7 T vs 9 T spec); 9-1-1 bore quoted as 74 mm (VTI, SRI 2022) vs 3 inches (7.5 cm, slides).

Whether dichroic ptychography/tomography is offered in general user mode (the directory lists 'dichroic imaging, 400 nm resolution' and 'dichroic ptychography' as techniques). Where the 4 m and 10 m ptychography detectors physically sit (possibly in 4-ID-H).
Contents and purpose of the legacy mini-hutch 4-ID-MH (50.5–52.8 m), and the hutch ceiling heights (PDR asked for 6 m at the magnet hutch).
